sections.html:
Each of Maine's 16 counties has its own probate court, and that court runs the process. Courts there handle the estates of deceased and missing persons, plus guardianships, trusts, name changes and adoptions. Start in the county of the decedent's last home.

The governing law is the Maine Probate Code, Title 18-C of the Maine Revised Statutes. Most estates begin with an application to the register of probate. The register can issue a written statement of informal probate under 18-C M.R.S. §3-302, but only after 120 hours have gone by since the death. It remains in force until a formal testacy proceeding replaces it.

Forms can be filed electronically. The e-filing fee is $7, and court fees, surcharges, newspaper publication and certified mail can add to the total. Clerks cannot advise you on the law, which is why families often hire a lawyer for anything beyond a plain estate.

Priority starts with whoever the will names, then moves down through the spouse, devisees, heirs and last of all creditors. The full ranking is in Section 3-203. Anyone 18 or older whom a court has not found unsuitable in a formal proceeding can serve.

  • The will's own choice, including a person nominated under a power the will grants, ranks first.
  • A spouse who also inherits under the will ranks next, followed by other devisees, then a spouse with no devise, then other heirs.
  • A creditor may ask to be appointed once forty-five days have gone by since death. If nothing has been opened six months after death, the State Tax Assessor may apply.
  • Anyone entitled to letters can nominate another person, and anyone can step aside with a written renunciation filed in court.

Objecting to an appointment requires a formal proceeding. When heirs fight over who should serve, the house usually sits until it is settled.

sections.h2: Selling the house without a judge's approval
sections.html:
Usually the representative can sell and never needs to ask a judge. Under §3-711, the representative gets the powers an absolute owner has over title, held in trust for creditors and other interested people, and can use them with no hearing or order unless the section says otherwise.

The biggest limit is a waiting period for heirs. Before any sale or transfer of an interest in estate real property, the representative must give those heirs notice at least 10 days ahead, unless the will lets the sale go forward without notice. Section 3-715 adds authority to mortgage or lease estate property, or to sell it privately or at auction on cash or credit terms, subject to anything the will or a formal court order provides.

A cash sale follows three steps: sign the purchase agreement, send the 10-day heir notice, then sign the deed at closing as personal representative. Read the will before you start, since a will can narrow or widen these powers.

sections.h2: The small estate affidavit and real estate
sections.html:
Maine offers an affidavit for collecting personal property, and personal property is all it covers. Section 3-1201 lets a successor use it when three things are true: the estate's total value after liens and encumbrances is no higher than $40,000 as adjusted for inflation, a month has run since the death, and nobody has a petition pending to appoint a personal representative.

Since the 2025 amendment, each county probate court posts the current inflation-adjusted figure on its website every year. The affidavit reaches debts owed to the dead person and property held by others. Title to a house is outside its reach, so an estate with a house needs a personal representative appointed the ordinary way.

sections.h2: Creditor deadlines and probate time limits
sections.html:
Claims are generally cut off nine months after death, or sooner if the notice period ends first. Under Section 3-803, a claim that arose before death is barred unless it is presented by the earlier of those two dates.

StepTime limit
Informal probate by the registerAt least 120 hours after death
Small estate affidavitA month after death, with the estate under $40,000 (inflation adjusted)
Notice to creditors by publicationTwo weekly notices, claims due 4 months after the first
Mailed notice to a known creditorThe later of 4 months from publication and 60 days from mailing
Claims arising before deathEarlier of 9 months or the notice period
Last date to open probateThree years from death, with exceptions

The notice is published weekly, twice, in a general-circulation newspaper serving the decedent's county. A mortgage or other lien survives the claims bar. The State can still pursue Medicaid reimbursement if it files within four months of notice.

sections.h2: How long can heirs wait to open probate?
sections.html:
Probate generally cannot be opened after three years from the date of death. Section 3-108 sets that limit and lists exceptions. One exception permits a late proceeding to confirm title when the first three years passed with no activity. In that case the representative's authority is limited, and only administration expenses can be claimed against the estate.

A contest of an informally probated will can be filed until the later of 12 months from informal probate or three years from death. Waiting that long narrows what a representative can do with the house, so heirs who plan to sell usually move well before the deadline.

sections.h2: Transfer tax, property tax and fees
sections.html:
An estate that sells owes the state transfer tax; an estate that distributes to an heir does not. The rate in 36 M.R.S. §4641-A is $2.20 for every $500 of value, and the buyer and seller each owe half. Section 4641-C carves out deeds of distribution under Title 18-C, parent-to-child deeds with no payment, and transfer-on-death deeds.

A deed of distribution hands the house to an heir. A deed from the representative to a stranger who pays for the house is a sale. The exemption list is silent on a representative who sells to a buyer, so ask the registry of deeds or an attorney how the deed should be drafted.

Property tax is fixed by who owned the property on April 1 (36 M.R.S. §502), so the estate owes that year's bill. Buyer and seller can then prorate across the town's fiscal year under §558. Our Maine property tax guide covers abatements and tax liens, and the homestead exemption page explains how a vacant inherited house can lose the exemption.

sections.h2: Problems heirs run into with inherited houses
sections.html:
• Heirs split over the choice of representative or over selling at all. Any objection to an appointment has to be brought as a formal proceeding.
  • The house has unpaid property tax. Maine uses tax lien mortgages. Where the owner left a probated will, a probate judge can grant up to 60 extra days to redeem once the will is allowed or disallowed (36 M.R.S. §943).
  • Nobody lives there and repairs slide. A representative may hold assets until distribution and may pay for repairs, but spending estate cash calls for a plan.
  • Heirs live out of state. Electronic filing helps, and a representative can sell without every heir present once the 10-day notice has gone out.

If the estate's house needs work, a cash buyer lets the representative skip repairs and staging and sell as-is. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on Maine estate properties, and accepting is the representative's call. Any figure comes only after we see the house.

A workable order: find the will and file it, get letters issued, order death certificates and ask the town for a tax payoff. Then send the 10-day heir notice before anyone signs a purchase agreement.

faqs.q: Can a Maine estate avoid probate?
faqs.a: Sometimes it can skip it. The §3-1201 affidavit covers estates of $40,000 or less (inflation adjusted), yet it only collects personal property. For a house, plan on a personal representative.
The probate court of the county where the decedent lived. You can e-file, and each of the 16 counties runs its own court.

faqs.q: Does a Maine representative need a judge's approval to sell?
faqs.a: Usually not. Section 3-711 gives the representative an owner's power over title, with one catch: heirs get at least 10 days' notice before the sale unless the will waives it.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims?
faqs.a: Nine months from death, or less if the notice period ends first. A published notice gives creditors 4 months from the first printing.

faqs.q: Is transfer tax due on an estate house sale?
faqs.a: Yes on a sale: $2.20 per $500 of value, shared by buyer and seller. A Title 18-C deed of distribution to an heir is exempt.
